5	**MEMORANDUM ON THE SALLOW CREEK VIADUCT**

7	**Subject: the center-span bearings, milepost 22, Cadder Valley branch — their behavior prior to the rehabilitation of March 1954, and the mechanism of the phenomenon reported in the valley over that period.**
8

The structure at milepost 22 has been the subject of a local tradition of long standing, and that tradition has lately been the subject of inquiry by persons outside this office. The condition which produced the phenomenon was removed in 1954 and cannot recur. It is nevertheless considered proper that the mechanism be set down once, in writing, in a place where it can afterward be found, so that the office is not obliged to reconstruct it a second time from the same papers.
10	
11	**2. Sources.** The contract drawings for the viaduct are held here. The records of the 1954 rehabilitation are held here. A copy of the survey report made in September 1962, at the draw-down of the creek for the state's flood-control cut, is on the file, together with the cast pedestal recovered at that time. The account of the depot record is at second hand; the writer has not examined that book and has relied on what was reported of its contents. No witness has been interviewed and none is required. The behavior described below is not a matter of testimony.

13	**3. The structure.** Three spans: 120 feet, 300 feet, and 120 feet, five hundred and forty feet overall. The line reaches this point from the Ashby quarry at milepost 31 on a descending grade of 2.2 percent maintained over eight miles.
14	
15	**4. Bearing arrangement.** The north bearing of the center span is fixed. The south bearing was, as built, a nest of rollers seated in a cast pedestal, so that the whole of the span's movement with temperature was taken at the south end. In the rehabilitation of March 1954, undertaken to receive diesel power, the roller nest was taken out and rocker bearings affording four inches of travel each way were substituted. [tool_result: 1	# Retelling 10 — Wendell Frayne, notes for the family, 1971
2	
3	*Four typed pages left with the papers, so that the children will know who was who before there is nobody left to ask.*
4	
5	I am sixty-seven and the only one now who has the whole of this in his head, which is a poor reason to write anything down and the only reason I have. My mother was born in 1876. She died in 1959, at eighty-five, in the front room at Cadder Falls, and the black book was on the shelf over her chair where it had been since before I was born. I want to set out who these people were to one another, because I notice that the further off they get the more they slide together, and in twenty years somebody is going to tell one of you that your great-grandmother built the bridge, and you should be able to say what she actually did.

7	**The Rennicks.** My uncle Emil Rennick was born in 1866 and was a carpenter, and a good one. When the railroad put the viaduct across Sallow Creek he built the falsework — that is, the timber staging that the iron truss was put together on before it could stand by itself. It is a queer trade, building something whose whole purpose is to be taken down again, and he was proud of it in a way he was not proud of houses. He died in 1931.

She kept a book of her own, black oilcloth, alongside the company's book, and copied into hers what she thought was worth having twice. My uncle used to say she was the only person on the job who wrote down what happened rather than what was supposed to happen.
10	
11	**My father.** She married Josiah Frayne in 1902. He was a clerk at the mill and a mild, exact man; I was born in 1904 and he died in 1940. There were no other children.
